item.title: Arithmetic Depth, Minimal Gate Alphabets, and Exact Program-State Resources for Single-Qubit Dyadic Programs
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that for the entire family of single‑qubit “dyadic” rotations—those built from angles π/2^D—the deepest layer of exact resources can be identified analytically rather than bounded conservatively, collapsing gate count, field extension depth and program‑state complexity into a single minimal value. By proving a descent theorem that ties the Clifford‑cyclotomic tower to real cyclotomic fields, the authors give a rigorous certificate for optimal synthesis that complements recent advances in Clifford + T and other fixed‑alphabet compilers, promising tighter control of gate overhead on near‑term hardware where every non‑Clifford operation is costly. The result could streamline compiler pipelines and error‑budget calculations, though its current scope is limited to single‑qubit dyadic programs and will need extension before impacting multi‑qubit algorithm design.

Resource analyses for quantum programs commonly provide safe upper bounds on qubits, gates, or non-Clifford operations. We study a single-qubit dyadic fragment in which the deepest exact resource layer can instead be inferred exactly. Starting from the normalized-midpoint misty-state syntax, we define dyadic program states and the real cyclotomic tower $K_D=\mathbb Q(2\cos(π/2^D))$. For the projective single-qubit Clifford-cyclotomic tower $\widehat G_D\subseteq SO(3)$, we prove the relative intersection law $\widehat G_D\cap SO(3,K_d)=\widehat G_d$ for $d\le D$. Combining this descent theorem with an arithmetic-closure invariant for adaptive stabilizer processing yields $\mathrm{Fdepth}(U)=\mathrm{Adepth}(U)=\mathrm{Rdepth}(U)$: the smallest real cyclotomic field containing the Bloch matrix of an exactly synthesizable channel, the shallowest dyadic gate alphabet realizing it up to global phase, and the shallowest dyadic program-state layer sufficient for exact stabilizer-assisted implementation coincide. At that common minimum, known fixed-alphabet synthesis gives minimum primitive-rotation count. We package the result as an exact static resource effect and outline a certificate-producing compiler.

item.title: Optimal Holding Times for Entanglement Swapping
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a bottleneck in long‑distance quantum networking by showing how to set optimal memory holding times for heterogeneous repeater links, directly boosting the rate at which high‑fidelity entanglement can be swapped across a chain. By integrating realistic decoherence rates, multi‑memory capacities and classical latency into analytical throughput models, the work bridges the gap between abstract protocol design and the engineering constraints that recent fiber‑based and satellite QKD demonstrations are confronting. The resulting guidelines could help network architects tune hardware parameters to meet strict fidelity targets without over‑provisioning resources, though the benefits will depend on the specific memory technologies and link asymmetries in a given deployment.

We revisit the optimization of entanglement holding times in memory-based quantum repeaters for maximizing entanglement swapping throughput under different fidelity constraints - strict, probabilistic, and mean. We consider two heterogeneous quantum links that are equipped with single or multiple memories and differ in decoherence rates, memory capacities, entanglement attempt rates and success probabilities, as well as classical communication latencies. Efficient models are developed to estimate the expected entanglement throughput and the probability density functions of the conditional wait time to swap. The models are then used to satisfy different fidelity requirements by optimizing the maximum holding times for the two links. Finally, our proposed model and approach are validated with a discrete-event quantum network simulator.

item.title: Resource-efficient formulations of the Knapsack problem for quantum computing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the way a combinatorial problem is encoded for quantum hardware can be as important as the algorithm itself, demonstrating that more compact QUBO formulations of the classic Knapsack problem dramatically boost success rates on both LR‑QAOA simulations and D‑Wave annealers. By cutting slack variables or tightening penalty constants, the authors achieve several orders of magnitude higher optimal‑solution probabilities, a result that directly addresses one of the biggest bottlenecks—excess qubit overhead—in near‑term quantum optimization. The work therefore provides a practical template for other inequality‑constrained problems, suggesting that smarter encodings could unlock better performance from today’s noisy intermediate‑scale quantum devices.

Quantum computing has emerged as a new tool for solving combinatorial optimization problems. Quantum optimization approaches usually operate on the subclass of Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problems. Many optimization problems can be reformulated in this form, though there are often multiple ways to do so. The choice of formulation can considerably affect the performance of QUBO solvers in practice. In this work, we study QUBO formulations of the Knapsack problem, a canonical example of a problem with inequality constraints. In the standard formulation these constraints are converted into penalty terms, which requires additional slack variables. Here, we investigate three more resource-efficient approaches for formulating the Knapsack as a QUBO. The first two modify the standard formulation, either by deriving a smaller penalty constant or by reducing the number of slack variables. The third approach is a wholly different method, which avoids the use of slack variables entirely. All three approaches increase the probability of finding the optimal solution, both in simulations of the linear ramp Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (LR-QAOA) and on a D-Wave quantum annealer. The slackless method performs best, increasing success probabilities by several orders of magnitude even for relatively small problem sizes.

item.title: Solving a non-abelian hidden subgroup problem on a trapped-ion quantum computer: the power of the measurement basis
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first experimental realization of a non‑abelian hidden subgroup problem on a trapped‑ion processor, confirming that the choice of measurement basis—not just circuit depth—can be the decisive factor for quantum speed‑ups in problems such as graph isomorphism and lattice‑based cryptography. By testing weak, strong (adapted), adjacent‑pair, and forgetful sampling strategies on the IonQ Forte device, the authors show that theoretical predictions about when information can be extracted survive realistic noise levels, and even surpass an optimally tuned classical algorithm for a three‑query instance. The work demonstrates a concrete pathway toward quantum algorithms that exploit group structure beyond the abelian case, while reminding readers that scaling to larger groups will still demand improvements in qubit count and error rates.

The hidden subgroup problem (HSP) unifies many of the best-known quantum speed-ups. For abelian groups it is solved efficiently by weak Fourier sampling, but for non-abelian groups, which include the cases relevant to graph isomorphism and lattice-based cryptography, the right measurement basis is crucial and often unknown. We experimentally study the HSP over the $q$-hedral groups $\mathbb{Z}_q \ltimes \mathbb{Z}_p$, which interpolate between the dihedral and affine groups and mark a boundary between instances that are efficiently solvable and those that are only information-theoretically solvable. On the IonQ Forte trapped-ion quantum computer, with $p \le 7$, we implement weak Fourier sampling, strong Fourier sampling in an adapted basis, strong Fourier sampling of adjacent pairs, and forgetful abelian sampling. We demonstrate that the theoretical predictions of Moore, Rockmore, Russell and Schulman survive on a noisy device: weak sampling reveals nothing about the hidden subgroup, the adapted basis succeeds for large $q$, adjacent pairs succeed for small $q$, and forgetful sampling saturates below unit success. For $p=7$, $q=6$, the hardware exceeds the success probability of an exhaustively optimised classical algorithm for up to three oracle queries.

item.title: QASPA-MaxCut on Unweighted Graphs: Edge Encoding and QAOA Restarts
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces QASPA‑MaxCut, a novel edge‑encoding circuit that replaces the standard QAOA mixer with controlled R_y rotations and shows how a simple one‑layer ansatz can already match or exceed depth‑one QAOA on small unweighted graphs. By analytically deriving the two‑qubit algebra and demonstrating systematic gains through classical restarts, the work provides a concrete blueprint for low‑depth variational algorithms that are easier to implement on noisy hardware. The results suggest that careful circuit design and post‑selection can extract more performance from near‑term devices without increasing depth, though the findings are currently limited to exact simulations of very small graphs. Readers should watch how this approach scales, as it could reshape benchmark strategies for NISQ‑scale combinatorial optimization.

Max-Cut is a common testbed for near-term quantum optimization because it has a simple Ising Hamiltonian, established classical baselines, and a parameterized quantum circuit whose performance depends on the outer classical optimizer. This paper develops QASPA-MaxCut, a shift-phase circuit for Max-Cut that encodes graph edges through controlled $R_y$ rotations of the form $\mathrm{CX}_{ij}R_y(θ_{ij})\mathrm{CX}_{ij}$. We derive the exact two-qubit algebra of the edge block, trace an unweighted four-vertex example, and compare one-layer QASPA-MaxCut with depth-one QAOA by exact state-vector simulation. The protocol uses seed 42, evaluates connected backbone-augmented random graphs with additional-edge probabilities $p_{\mathrm{edge}}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7\}$, and adds nineteen custom unweighted topologies. The QASPA-MaxCut score is reported after the algorithm's classical selection stage: the four leading QASPA bit strings are evaluated by the Max-Cut objective, and the best cut is retained. The QAOA score is the expected approximation ratio after local optimization, reported as a best-of-$k$ curve over one to ten restarts. In these small exact simulations, fixed-angle QASPA-MaxCut produces reported group-mean selection ratios between $0.955$ and $1.000$, the topology-level readout is unchanged in the retained finite-shot checks under the rule $\lceil 0.03047\cdot 2^n+1016.2\rceil$, and depth-one QAOA improves with additional classical restarts while remaining lower than the QASPA selection score in the reported mean summaries. This comparison motivates further study of the classical search budget needed to obtain competitive Max-Cut samples at shallow circuit depth.

item.title: First-principles study of the formation of Group-IV--vacancy color centers in diamond
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints why the promising group‑IV–vacancy (SiV, GeV, SnV, PbV) color centers often appear at far lower concentrations than ion‑implantation doses would suggest: competing capture of carbon interstitials or extra vacancies readily converts the split‑vacancy configuration into less useful defects. By quantifying binding energies, diffusion barriers and charge transition levels with first‑principles calculations, the authors show that controlling the Fermi level during annealing could suppress these side reactions and boost the yield of optically active spin qubits. The insight dovetails with recent experimental pushes to engineer high‑purity diamond platforms for quantum networking, offering a concrete materials‑science lever to improve device reproducibility.

$XV$ ($X$ is Si, Ge, Sn, or Pb, and $V$ is the carbon vacancy) color centers are promising platforms for quantum computing and quantum information science due to their favorable optical and spin properties. They are commonly fabricated by ion implantation, which inevitably introduces vacancies and carbon self-interstitials (C$_i$) into the lattice. However, the microscopic formation mechanism remains unclear, limiting the yield and stability of $XV$ centers. Here, first-principles calculations are conducted to systematically investigate the roles of $V$ and C$_i$ in $XV$ formation. We find that $XV$ formation is energetically favorable, with large binding energies and low diffusion barriers. Nevertheless, $XV$ readily captures C$_i$ to form substitutional defect $X_s$, or captures an additional $V$ to form the complex $XV_2$. Charge transition levels show that oppositely charged reactants never meet in these reactions, and that Coulomb repulsion blocks them only when both reactants carry charges of the same sign, which for the capture of C$_i$ requires strongly n- or p-type conditions. These competing defect reactions destabilize the split-vacancy configuration and could account for the low formation yield of $XV$ centers, so that they appear at concentrations well below those expected from the implanted dose. Our results elucidate the microscopic origin of this intrinsic instability and suggest that Fermi-level control may suppress defect conversions and stabilize the split-vacancy configuration.

item.title: Flux Crosstalk Calibration from Zero Knowledge to High Precision in Fully Tunable Superconducting Circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles one of the thorniest bottlenecks for scaling superconducting quantum processors—flux‑crosstalk between tunable qubits and couplers—by introducing calibration techniques that work without any prior spectroscopy or dedicated readout lines. By leveraging intrinsic coupler‑resonator interactions, the zero‑knowledge method speeds up chip bring‑up, while the symmetric branch cancellation scheme pushes residual crosstalk down to below 5 × 10⁻⁵, a precision level needed for error‑corrected operation. Together they give hardware teams a practical pathway from initial device turn‑on to the fine‑grained control required for large‑scale, fully tunable architectures.

Precise and independent flux control is essential for scalable superconducting processors built from frequency-tunable qubits and couplers, but flux crosstalk undermines it. Conventional calibration methods rely either on dedicated readout channels, which tunable couplers typically lack, or on readout schemes requiring extensive prior spectroscopy of the qubit and coupler. We demonstrate two independent methods that characterize coupler flux crosstalk without directly driving or measuring the couplers. The first method is zero-knowledge characterization, which exploits intrinsic coupler-resonator coupling to yield rapid and accurate estimates with no prior qubit or coupler spectroscopy, accelerating large scale bring-up. The second method is symmetric branch cancellation, which isolates crosstalk from other dispersive effects allowing for quantifying with high precision. Combined with an improved iterative procedure, these methods suppress residual coupler crosstalk below $5\times10^{-5}$, providing a complete route from zero-knowledge initialization to high-precision crosstalk characterization in fully tunable architectures.

item.title: Efficient quantum ultraspherical transform and a well-conditioned quantum spectral method
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first fully efficient quantum circuit for ultraspherical transforms beyond the cosine‑ and sine‑case, showing that a polynomial‑in‑log N gate count suffices to switch between pointwise amplitudes and spectral coefficients for any fixed integer order m≥2. By coupling this transform with a well‑conditioned preconditioning strategy, the authors construct a quantum spectral solver whose linear‑system condition numbers remain bounded, extending recent quantum linear‑equation algorithms into the realm of high‑accuracy differential‑equation simulation. The result narrows a key practical gap—efficiently preparing and manipulating smooth function representations on a quantum computer—bringing hardware‑friendly quantum PDE solvers one step closer to real‑world applications.

Solving differential equations is a promising application of quantum computing. Spectral methods, where the solution is represented by coefficients in a basis, are particularly well suited to quantum solvers because their structured discretizations can enable efficient linear-algebra operations while providing rapid convergence. Their quantum implementation, however, requires an efficient transform between amplitudes encoding function values and amplitudes encoding expansion coefficients. This work develops two key components of a quantum spectral method. First, we construct the quantum ultraspherical transform (QUT) for orthonormal ultraspherical polynomials, a basis that supports sparse and well-conditioned discretizations of differential equations. For the basis parameters $m=0$ and $1$, this transform reduces to the discrete cosine and sine transforms with known efficient circuits. Our contribution covers every fixed integer $m\geq2$: for dimensions $N$ with $N+m=2^n$, where $n$ is the number of qubits, the QUT achieves error at most $\varepsilon$ using a gate count polynomial in $n$ and $\log(1/\varepsilon)$. The construction builds on the quantum Fourier transform, augmented by approximations whose accuracy guarantees are independent of $N$. Second, we develop a quantum spectral solver for regular linear ordinary differential equations based on the QUT. Under suitable boundary conditions and data-access assumptions, preconditioning keeps condition numbers bounded independently of the basis size, allowing the solution state to be prepared at polylogarithmic cost in system size and inverse error. Together, these contributions provide a framework for quantum spectral methods with the potential to solve linear differential equations efficiently.

item.title: Parrondo's paradox for three discrete-time quantum walks with distinct shift operators
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article expands the toolbox for discrete‑time quantum walks by showing that Parrondo’s paradox can be realized with a single coin but three distinct shift operators, opening a new route to engineer counterintuitive transport behavior without complex coin sequences. By linking the paradox to the evolution of walker–coin entanglement, it provides fresh insight into how bias reversal can be harnessed for dynamic control in quantum algorithms and simulation protocols. The work also highlights that richer shift dynamics—beyond simple left/right moves—may become a practical lever for designing more versatile quantum walk‑based processors, though experimental implementation will need to address the added hardware complexity of multi‑outcome shifts.

Parrondo's paradox describes a surprising phenomenon in which certain combinations of biased quantum walks result in an unexpected reversal of their bias direction. To date, research on this effect has predominantly focused on one-dimensional discrete-time quantum walks that employ fixed sequences of two or three quantum coins, paired with a single shift operator. In this work, we first introduce a wide class of unitary shift operators which allow for three movement options (left, right or stay in place) of a walker in one time step, and we then demonstrate that Parrondo's paradox can also arise with a single coin and three distinct shift operators. Furthermore, we investigate how this paradox influences the time evolution of quantum entanglement between the walker and the coin in such quantum walks.

item.title: A Variational Quantum Algorithm for Multi-Skill Project Scheduling
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a concrete pathway for using variational quantum algorithms on near‑term hardware to tackle the notoriously hard multi‑skill project scheduling problem that underpins many real‑world logistics and workforce planning tasks. By introducing a temporal batch decomposition and a logarithmic binary encoding that keep each subproblem within 30 qubits, the authors show how to sidestep the exponential Hilbert‑space blow‑up while still exploring whether entanglement actually aids training on an otherwise classical QUBO ground state. The systematic comparison of hardware‑efficient ansätze with an entanglement‑free baseline provides early evidence that modest quantum resources could complement classical heuristics, though scalability beyond the simulated instances and mitigation of barren plateaus remain open challenges.

Job scheduling is an NP-hard optimization problem with clear industrial relevance. In practice, distributing work across a team is not only about meeting deadlines or improving productivity; it also affects fatigue, stress, and employee well-being. Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) provide a promising way to address these problems through QUBO formulations, although their scalability on near-term NISQ hardware is still limited by Hilbert-space growth and barren plateaus. In this work, we simulate a VQA for a realistic Multi-Skill Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (MS-RCPSP), including worker capacities, skill matrices, task priorities, deadlines, and calendar stability during rescheduling. To keep the problem within a near-term circuit size, we use a temporal batch decomposition that solves one day at a time, propagates the remaining workload, and combines it with a logarithmic binary encoding that keeps every batch at or below 30 qubits. Because the ground state of a QUBO Hamiltonian is a computational basis state, entanglement is not required to represent the solution, raising the question of whether it helps or hinders ansatz training. We address this question by comparing the linear and brick-wall entangling topologies of a hardware-efficient ansatz with an entanglement-free reference that has the same number of parameters and by training every configuration with COBYLA and with Adam using SPSA gradient estimation. For the instance and initialization studied, the entanglement-free reference produced feasible schedules under both optimizers. With COBYLA, it produced the feasible schedule closest to the required workload at a fraction of the simulation cost of the entangled topologies, indicating that entanglement did not improve the solutions found by the VQA.

item.title: Improved Exact and Approximate Quantum Fourier Transforms from Multiplication
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that by leveraging state‑of‑the‑art integer‑multiplication techniques the quantum Fourier transform can be implemented with only O(q log q) gates, a dramatic reduction from the classic O(q²) and even the previous Cleve–Watrous bound. Because QFT underpins Shor’s factoring, phase estimation and many newer algorithms, tighter gate counts translate directly into shallower circuits that are far more realistic on near‑term hardware. The authors also point out that any future breakthrough in classical multiplication—such as the recent OpenAI claim of sub‑linear‑logarithmic complexity—would immediately push QFT below O(q log q), opening a path to ultra‑efficient quantum arithmetic. The result is primarily theoretical at present, but it establishes a clear roadmap for turning advances in classical algorithms into concrete quantum speedups.

In the world of quantum computing, quantum Fourier transform (QFT) has been one of the most important subroutines for quantum algorithms, as exemplified by Shor's factoring algorithms and phase estimation (which in itself has been used as a primitive in various quantum algorithms). In fact most of the well known quantum algorithms can be divided into two classes, QFT based algorithms and search based algorithms. The usual circuit for QFT (covered in almost every basic quantum algorithms course) needs $O(q^2)$ gates (and $O(q)$ qubits) to perform the exact Fourier transform over $\mathbb{F}_{2^q}$. Cleve and Watrous (FOCS 2000) improved this gate count to $O(q (\log q)^2 (\log \log q))$ using the integer multiplication algorithm in $O(n (\log n) (\log \log n))$ time for two $n$-bit integers (best known at that time). Our first main result shows that this gate count can be improved to $O(q (\log q))$. In fact, if there is a multiplication circuit, to multiply two $n$-bit integers, with $O(n (\log n)^α)$ gates; we get a QFT circuit with $O(q (\log q)^α)$ gates (improving upon $O(q (\log q)^{α+ 1})$) gates from the construction of Cleve and Watrous). Given the recent claim by OpenAI about integer multiplication, this opens up the possibility of having a QFT circuit with $o \left( q (\log q)\right)$ gates. On approximating the QFT over $\ZZ/(2^q \ZZ)$, the result of Ahokas, Cleve and Hales (ERATO 2003) showed that an approximating circuit can be built with $O \left( q (\log \log(q/\varepsilon))^{α+1} \right)$ gates, where $ε$ is the approximating parameter. Our second main result again improves this to $O \left( q (\log \log(q/\varepsilon))^α \right)$ gates.

item.title: Semi-Device-Independent Certification of multi-qubit Entangled Basis Measurement
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a semi‑device‑independent protocol that can certify multi‑qubit entangled basis measurements using only a prepare‑and‑measure setup, offering a practical alternative to full tomography for hardware verification. By framing the problem in a classical causal‑model language and deriving nonlinear witnesses whose quantum optimum surpasses classical limits, the work extends recent self‑testing advances into the multipartite regime that underpins teleportation, dense coding and entanglement swapping. The ability to certify both the measurement and the prepared states with minimal assumptions could accelerate scaling of quantum networking nodes and sensing platforms, although the method currently relies on a specific tripartite scenario and trusted state preparation.

The entangled basis measurement plays a pivotal role in fundamental information-processing tasks, such as dense coding, quantum teleportation, and entanglement swapping. Consequently, certifying such measurements in a device-independent manner remains an important task. In this work, we present a semi-device-independent (SDI) protocol in a prepare-and-measure (PM) scenario for certifying a class of m-qubit entangled basis measurements. Specifically, we consider a tripartite PM scenario featuring two senders and one receiver, where each sender sends an arbitrary number of 2^m inputs and the receiver performs a measurement with 2^m outcomes. We adopt a classical causal model framework to demonstrate the non-classicality of quantum measurements. We introduce nonlinear witnesses in classical causal models and demonstrate that the optimal quantum value exceeds the classical bounds. Further, we demonstrate that the optimal quantum value of the witness SDI certify the entangled basis measurement and the prepared states of the two senders.

item.title: Spatial Path Superposition: A No-Cloning Perspective on MIMO-Inspired Spatial Diversity
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article spotlights spatial path superposition as a genuinely quantum analogue of classical MIMO diversity, turning the no‑cloning restriction into an advantage by delocalising a single qubit across multiple channels in coherent superposition. By showing that such superposed routes can boost fidelity and even generate bipartite or multipartite entanglement despite noisy propagation, it offers a new primitive for building robust quantum‑internet links that complement recent work on multiplexed quantum repeaters and error‑corrected photonic networks. The proposal is especially timely as experimental platforms—integrated photonics, fiber bundles, and free‑space satellite links—are reaching the control needed to maintain coherence across parallel paths, though practical deployment will still hinge on precise phase stabilization and loss management.

Spatial diversity is a key mechanism in classical Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) communications, where multiple propagation alternatives provide redundant observations that improve reliability in noisy environments. A direct translation of this principle to quantum communications is forbidden by the no-cloning theorem, since an unknown quantum state cannot be copied and transmitted through independent links. In this Perspective article, we argue that spatial path superposition provides a no-cloning-compatible analogue of the spatial-diversity principle of MIMO. Rather than duplicating the transmitted quantum state, a quantum carrier is coherently delocalized over multiple communication links, so that alternative spatial evolutions are experienced in quantum superposition. In this framework, classical redundancy is replaced by spatial coherence, and the communication link itself becomes part of the quantum dynamics. Indeed, spatial coherence can enhance the fidelity of the received quantum state, providing the quantum counterpart of the classical diversity gain, and can be converted into bipartite and multipartite entanglement during propagation. This implies that, under suitable coherent path control, noisy channel evolutions can contribute constructively to entanglement generation. This Perspective identifies spatial path superposition as a quantum-native primitive for the Quantum Internet, linking no-cloning-compatible spatial diversity, fidelity enhancement, entanglement generation, and coherent path control.

item.title: Bridging Pulse and Circuit Levels: A Geometric Framework for Deterministic Error Suppression
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a deterministic, ancilla‑free error‑suppression technique that translates the geometric pulse‑level approach to the discrete circuit layer, achieving an O(1) bound on coherent error growth instead of the √N scaling typical of randomized compiling. By actively shaping error trajectories with optimized twirling sequences, it offers a hardware‑efficient bridge between continuous robust control and digital compilation—an advance that could tighten error budgets on near‑term devices before full fault tolerance arrives. The work complements recent pulse‑shaping efforts and suggests a practical path for extending circuit depth without the massive qubit overhead of conventional quantum error correction.

Quantum errors in noisy environments remain a major obstacle to advancing quantum information technology. Standard quantum error correction requires massive ancillary qubit overhead, motivating the need for hardware-efficient mitigation strategies. In this work, we propose a framework for dynamical quantum error correction at the circuit level, requiring no logical encoding or ancillary qubits. By extending a geometric framework (originally developed for creating dynamical error-correcting gates at the control pulse level) to the discrete dynamics of digital circuits, we map the accumulation of coherent errors to trajectories in a high-dimensional error space. We demonstrate that inserting deterministically optimized twirling gate sequences actively shapes these trajectories, utilizing destructive interference to keep the accumulated error bounded with error scaling $\mathcal{O}(1)$. This deterministic path-shaping suppresses circuit errors fundamentally differently than the stochastic random-walk behavior of standard randomized compiling with error scaling $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})$. Furthermore, we show that this circuit-level dynamical correction synergizes with pulse-level robust control, providing an analytical bridge between continuous noise dynamics and discrete quantum compilation. This research illuminates pathways to achieving highly noise-resistant quantum circuits prior to the era of fault tolerance.

item.title: Connection of surface code patches based on entanglement distillation without postselection
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that surface‑code patches can be linked across a network using entanglement distillation that avoids the cumbersome postselection step, removing a major engineering bottleneck for distributed fault‑tolerant processors. By demonstrating through simulation that logical error rates improve—and can be further lowered by exploiting the inherent spacelike/timelike asymmetry of surface‑code errors—the work bridges a gap between theoretical protocols and hardware‑friendly implementations. If these techniques scale to larger lattices, they could enable modular quantum computers that grow by stitching together smaller, well‑controlled nodes rather than building monolithic chips.

Distributed quantum computing is a promising approach for overcoming the scalability limitations of fault-tolerant quantum computing. Entanglement distillation, a process that extracts higher-fidelity entangled states from noisy ones, plays a key role in distributed quantum computing. However, simple distillation protocols typically rely on postselection, which poses practical challenges for implementation. Here, we propose a scheme for distributed surface-code quantum computing that benefits from entanglement distillation even without postselection. Numerical simulations show that the logical error rates in the proposed scheme are lower than those in the setting without distillation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the logical error rates can be suppressed further by exploiting the asymmetry between spacelike and timelike errors in the surface code. The proposed scheme offers a practical and simple approach to distributed quantum computing with surface codes.

item.title: Resetting a Superconducting Qubit with a Compact Colder Resistive Dissipator below the Qubit Frequency
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a compact on‑chip resistive dissipator that can cool a superconducting transmon from 49 mK to 35 mK and reset it with a process error of just 0.28 %, all without adding extra control lines or degrading the qubit’s T₁. Efficient qubit reset has become a key requirement for large-scale superconducting quantum processors, as initialization fidelity increasingly lags behind gate performance and quantum error correction demands rapid, high-fidelity state re-initialization. This work proposes a compact on-chip dissipator consisting of two transmon dissipation modes and a thin-film resistor, and experimentally demonstrates an unconditional reset protocol. With no additional control lines and negligible impact on the qubit $T_1$, the effective temperature of the transmon qubit is reduced from $49$~mK to $35$~mK. Quantum process tomography is employed to benchmark the reset process, achieving a process error of $0.0028$. This reset protocol is robust to pulse parameter deviations, thereby relaxing calibration requirements. The dissipator architecture provides a practical, calibration-friendly reset solution for large-scale superconducting quantum processors.

item.title: Robust Geometric Gates for QCCD Architecture
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that non‑cyclic geometric single‑qubit gates can dramatically suppress the shuttling‑induced noise that has long limited QCCD‑based trapped‑ion processors, delivering gate fidelities well above those of conventional dynamical pulses even when ions are moved repeatedly. By validating the approach on a planar chip trap with up to 33 qubits, the work shows that robust geometric control scales alongside the ion‑shuttle architecture, bringing truly plug‑and‑play quantum primitives within reach for large‑scale ion‑based computers. The result bridges a critical gap between high‑fidelity stationary gates and the flexible connectivity required for fault‑tolerant QCCD systems, although further integration with two‑qubit operations will be needed to complete a full error‑corrected stack.

The trapped-ion quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) is a promising route toward scalable quantum computing. However, the frequency offset during shuttling operations introduce significant decoherence and control errors, severely degrading gate fidelity on transported ions. Here, using a room-temperature planar chip trap, we demonstrate a robust and universal single-qubit gate set in the QCCD architecture. Based on a recently proposed path-optimizable noncyclic geometric scheme, we show that dynamic noise is strongly suppressed even when multiple shuttling operations are interleaved with gate execution, achieving substantially higher fidelities than conventional dynamical gates. This robustness is further validated in a multi-ion system containing up to 33 qubits. With inherent robustness and adaptability to varying shuttle distances and ion numbers, our work offers a plug-and-play solution for building robust quantum primitives for the QCCD platform.

item.title: Quantum Error Correction in Nearly Critical Toric Codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that topological error‑correction can remain robust even as a toric code is driven right up to its quantum critical point, demonstrating a finite decoding threshold for both bit‑flip and phase‑flip noise when the transverse field is infinitesimally close to the transition. By exploiting the stoquastic nature of the transverse‑field toric Hamiltonian, the authors devise an optimal post‑measurement decoder that can be implemented efficiently with Monte Carlo simulations of a constrained lattice gauge theory—an approach that bridges quantum many‑body physics and practical fault‑tolerance. The result suggests that future quantum memories could tolerate stronger perturbations than previously thought, though the technique currently applies only to stoquastic deformations of stabilizer codes.

We investigate quantum error correction protocols for topological codes deformed away from their stabilizer limits, particularly as they are pushed towards quantum phase transitions into trivial phases. Our focus is primarily on quantum information stored within the ground-state manifold of the transverse-field toric code (TFTC), subjected to independent bit-flip and phase-flip decoherence. Although the transverse field induces strong quantum fluctuations of $m$ anyons in the ground states, we show that projective measurements of the "bare" toric code stabilizers can nevertheless be used to construct an efficient decoding algorithm which exhibits a finite threshold to both types of decoherence, even when the transverse field is tuned infinitesimally close to the quantum critical point. Our construction of the optimal postmeasurement decoders---that is, the optimal decoders assuming that the stabilizers are first measured---crucially relies on the stoquastic nature of the TFTC Hamiltonian, which affords a description of its ground states in terms of a classical lattice gauge theory. Using stoquasticity, we first prove that stabilizer measurements act unitarily on the undecohered TFTC ground states to excellent approximation, and that the optimal postmeasurement decoder can be efficiently implemented via Monte Carlo simulation of a constrained lattice gauge theory. We then construct the optimal postmeasurement decoder for the TFTC states under bit-flip and phase-flip decoherence, where we numerically demonstrate a finite threshold close to the quantum critical point. We provide theoretical evidence (without a rigorous proof) that stabilizer measurements constitute an optimal decoding strategy in this setting. For phase-flip decoherence, we further prove that the optimal postmeasurement decoding threshold is independent of the transverse field strength throughout the topological phase.

item.title: Quantum Advantage has Few Complexity Implications
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the existence of “proofs of quantumness” or oblivious state‑preparation protocols does not automatically force a separation between classical and quantum complexity classes, even in worlds where P = NP or BQP = QCMA. By constructing explicit classical and unitary oracles, the authors demonstrate that such quantum advantage tests can coexist with surprisingly weak separations, which tempers expectations that they will directly yield new post‑quantum cryptographic primitives via relativizing proofs. The result sharpens our understanding of what recent experimental demonstrations of quantumness can (and cannot) guarantee for future security constructions.

We consider the complexity implications of proofs of quantumness and (quantum verifier) oblivious state preparation. We show that both of these objects can coexist with the easiness of nondeterministic computation. That is, we give evidence that proofs of quantumness can exist when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{NP}$ and that (quantum verifier) oblivious state preparation can exist when $\mathsf{BQP} = \mathsf{QCMA}$. In particular, we give a classical oracle relative to which (1) $\mathsf{P}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{NP}^\mathcal{O}$ (2) $\mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{PSPACE}^\mathcal{O}$ (3) Proofs of quantumness exist. In particular, there exists a language in $\mathsf{IP}^\mathcal{O} \subseteq \mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O}$ which is hard on average against $\mathsf{P}^\mathcal{O}/poly$. We give a unitary oracle such that (1) $\mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{QCMA}^\mathcal{O}$ (2) Quantum verifier oblivious state preparation exists. These oracle separations directly imply a number of related consequences. For example, our first result implies that proofs of quantumness cannot be used to construct classical or quantum cryptography with a relativizing proof. Our second result implies that quantum computation/classical communication oblivious transfer cannot be used to construct post-quantum one-way functions with a relativizing proof.

item.title: DynaMite: Dynamic Measurement Scheduling To Accelerate Fault-Tolerant Quantum Programs
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles one of the biggest hidden bottlenecks in fault‑tolerant processors: the static measurement latency that inflates logical cycle times and error rates. By introducing DynaMite’s real‑time latency selection, which tailors readout speed to each logical cycle’s error budget, the authors show a clear path to shave tens of percent off both runtime and logical error probability—an advance that dovetails with recent efforts in active reset and low‑latency control stacks from IBM and Google. If hardware can expose fast, programmable measurement windows, the technique could become a practical lever for scaling up surface‑code or other QEC codes without waiting for fundamentally faster detectors.

Fault-tolerant quantum computers run millions of logical cycles to perform quantum error correction (QEC). As logical operations span entire logical cycles, the logical cycle time (LCT) dictates program runtime. Qubit measurements, critical to extract parity information for QEC, are the slowest operations and account for 43-86% of LCT. Measurement latencies impact fidelity: fast measurements lower our ability to correctly classify quantum states, whereas slow measurements increase the likelihood of decoherence. Hardware providers thus calibrate measurement latencies that maximize readout fidelity per qubit and use them to schedule all measurements during program execution. However, calibrated latencies are sub-optimal for logical performance because logical cycles span multiple QEC rounds, during which data qubits are not measured. This increases LCT and logical error rates (LERs) due to decoherence at the logical level. We propose DynaMite, a lightweight real-time measurement latency selection policy built on two key insights. First, logical cycles must use a measurement latency that is fast enough to reduce both LCT and LER for the QEC code, instead of the calibrated latency that only maximizes readout fidelity. Second, not all logical cycles are equal; many do not fully utilize the error budget of the QEC code, i.e., the number of failed parity checks it can tolerate without compromising LER. These cycles could use even faster measurements but do not, because latencies are chosen statically, whereas error information is only available at runtime. DynaMite exploits the fact that a logical cycle comprises multiple QEC rounds and selects the fastest latency for an upcoming round based on the error budget left and rounds remaining. Our evaluations show that DynaMite reduces LCT by 1.69x on average and up to 2.29x, and reduces LER to 0.46x on average and up to 0.13x of baseline.

item.title: Data informed Ansatz Selection for Variational Quantum Circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This work shows that the architecture of variational quantum circuits can be chosen deterministically from the data itself rather than by costly trial‑and‑error searches, a step that could dramatically shrink the overhead of VQC design on near‑term hardware. By linking Fourier coefficient ranks to entanglement needs and using the growth law of the quantum Fisher information matrix to set depth, the authors provide concrete, analytically grounded rules that complement recent efforts to automate ansatz construction and reduce barren‑plateau risk. The demonstrated 78 % accuracy on a benchmark dataset without any hyperparameter sweep suggests a practical pathway for scaling VQCs to larger problems while keeping experimental resources in check, though performance will still depend on the quality of data encoding and hardware noise levels.

Choosing a variational quantum circuit (VQC) usually means searching over ansatze and depths, and training each candidate. We give three rules that fix these choices from the data and the gate set alone, before any training. First, a circuit without entangling gates has a rank-one Fourier coefficient tensor on every subset of qubits. A singular value decomposition of a dataset's Fourier coefficients therefore indicates whether entanglement is needed, which qubits it connects, and a lower bound on the error of omitting it. Second, the rank of the quantum Fisher information matrix grows by $p_0$ per layer, after a first-layer deficit $d_0$, until it reaches a ceiling set by the dynamical Lie algebra. This law fixes the depth. Third, reading out all $2^N - 1$ Pauli-Z products from one batch of shots resolves half of the state's directions, the most any single-basis readout can. A single-qubit readout resolves an exponentially small fraction. For the Madelon dataset, the rules prescribe 7 blocks of 3 qubits at depth 3: a 239-parameter classifier with 78.5% test accuracy, found without a grid search. Ablations confirm three predicted effects: shallower circuits, smaller blocks and dropping reuploading all lower accuracy.

item.title: QECert: Formal Foundations for Quantum Error-Correction Theory in Lean
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it brings the rigor of interactive theorem proving to quantum error‑correction theory, giving researchers a machine‑checked foundation for the increasingly complex constructions that underpin scalable fault tolerance. By encoding stabilizer, CSS and modern LDPC code families—including hypergraph‑product and quantum Tanner codes—in Lean, QECert lets developers verify asymptotic parameter bounds, Bravyi‑Poulin‑Terhal limits and magic‑state overheads with confidence, a step that aligns with the recent surge of high‑performance LDPC designs for near‑term devices. The library’s reusable formalism could accelerate both theoretical advances and practical compiler or architecture verification, though its impact will depend on broader adoption within the quantum community.

Quantum error correction provides the mathematical basis for protecting quantum information against noise. Existing formalizations have established foundations for stabilizer codes and code verification. However, a systematic formal treatment of the asymptotic constructions and fundamental limitations that underpin scalable quantum error correction is still needed. We present QECert, a Lean library providing reusable formal foundations for these theoretical questions. It connects quantum error-correction criteria, stabilizer and Calderbank-Shor-Steane codes, and algebraic and homological constructions within a common framework. Asymptotically good quantum low density parity check codes provide the principal case study. We formalize constructions and asymptotic parameter theorems spanning hypergraph products, balanced products, lifted products, and quantum Tanner codes. Further developments cover Bravyi-Poulin-Terhal bounds and related locality restrictions, constant overhead magic state distillation, and energy barriers and storage errors for quantum memories. QECert establishes a reusable formal foundation for studying the capabilities, resource requirements, and fundamental limitations of quantum error correction, supporting systematic verification and further development of its theory.

item.title: Reopening the one clean qubit case of a semi-grand challenge
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article revives a long‑standing open problem by showing that the previously accepted proof that “one clean qubit” circuits stay classically simulable is flawed, exposing a concrete counterexample that still respects full separability yet evades the claimed simulation form. By pinpointing the gap in Aaronson’s 2005 semi‑grand challenge argument, it forces theorists to re‑examine the boundary between efficiently simulable mixed‑state models and genuinely quantum advantage—an issue now especially relevant as experimental groups explore DQC1‑style processors with noisy registers. Although the new circuits themselves are easy to simulate, the work underscores that a definitive answer to whether separable mixed‑state computation can be classically tractable remains unsettled, keeping the question alive for future algorithmic and complexity‑theoretic breakthroughs.

In his 2005 list of semi-grand challenges for quantum computing theory, Scott Aaronson asked whether a quantum computer that is always in a separable mixed state can be simulated by a classical computer in polynomial time. An affirmative answer was claimed for the one clean qubit model of quantum computation. The supporting mathematical arguments relied on an exhaustive characterization of circuits that stay in separable states. Here, we give a counterexample where one pure qubit, known as the clean qubit, controls a sequence of three gates that act on a maximally mixed three-qubit register. The overall unitary that accumulates as these gates are applied has the properties that ensure the state of all four qubits remains fully separable. Crucially, we show that the final unitary cannot be put into the form required by the claimed simulation result. We also give a continuous-time implementation of the same circuit that keeps the qubits fully separable throughout and ends at the same unitary. We extend our counterexamples to a uniform family, and pinpoint the gap in the earlier proof. Since our circuits are themselves efficient to simulate classically, this work does not settle Aaronson's question. It does, however, reopen the semi-grand challenge for an actively researched model of quantum computation.

item.title: Recoverability of Gravitational Entanglement under Decoherence
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the disappearance of a measurable gravitational‑entanglement signal under realistic noise does not mean the underlying quantum resource is gone – strictly local quantum error‑correction can amplify the effective Newtonian coupling relative to residual decoherence for GRW and CSL collapse models, even when the raw entanglement appears vanishing. By contrast, the Diósi–Penrose model resists such recovery, highlighting a concrete way to discriminate between competing theories of gravity‑induced decoherence with near‑term tabletop experiments. The work therefore bridges recent proposals to witness gravity‑mediated entanglement and practical error‑mitigation techniques, suggesting that clever encoding could keep quantum‑gravity signatures alive despite environmental noise.

Decoherence can make gravitationally generated entanglement arbitrarily small, or even vanishing, without necessarily rendering the effective matter dynamics separable. We ask whether this hidden non-separability can be revealed using strictly local quantum error correction. For Newtonian gravity supplemented by physically relevant localization noise, including environmental noise, and noise from collapse models such as GRW, CSL, and Diósi--Penrose, we analyze when the underlying entangling resource is locally recoverable. For GRW- and CSL-type noise, we analytically establish that strictly local quantum error correction can make the ratio of the effective gravitational interaction strength to the residual decoherence rate arbitrarily large for any parametrization of the collapse model, even in regimes where the unencoded entanglement signal approaches zero. By contrast, the Diósi--Penrose model does not exhibit the same enhancement under bipartite protocol considered here, revealing a qualitative difference. These results show that the loss of detectable entanglement is not equivalent to the loss of a recoverable non-separable resource, and open a route toward practical recovery protocols.

item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows the first practical use‑case where a noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) processor can beat state‑of‑the‑art classical models on a real‑world financial forecasting task, highlighting quantum reservoir computing as a latency‑friendly way to harness large qubit arrays. By leveraging Rigetti’s 108‑qubit chip, FirstQFM demonstrates that even without full fault tolerance, quantum‑enhanced time‑series analysis can deliver higher Sharpe ratios and profit metrics than leading machine‑learning baselines. The result builds on recent work exploring hybrid quantum‑classical learning architectures and suggests a near‑term pathway for quant firms to experiment with NISQ hardware, though the advantage remains task‑specific and does not yet constitute a universal quantum speedup.

FirstQFM, in collaboration with SW7 Group and Rigetti Computing, has successfully demonstrated a financial forecasting pilot using quantum reservoir computing (QRC) on Rigetti’s 108-qubit processor. This QRC system outperformed classical machine learning models and time-series foundation models in financial benchmarks, achieving significantly higher cumulative gross profit and loss and Sharpe ratios. The study highlights QRC as a promising and latency-efficient approach for deploying NISQ processors in quantitative finance, despite not claiming general quantum advantage. item.title: Band structure of two-dimensional graphene and of one-dimensional nanoribbons via variational quantum algorithms: from energies to wavefunction quality
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that a single variational workflow can map the band structure of realistic graphene sheets and nanoribbons onto current NISQ hardware, showing how VQE and its deflation extension can retrieve both ground‑state and excited‑state dispersions with only logarithmic qubit scaling. By quantifying how circuit depth trades off between ideal accuracy and noise‑induced error, the work provides a practical benchmark for future materials‑focused quantum simulations and highlights the need for deeper, lower‑error devices before truly predictive calculations become feasible.

Simulating quantum many-body systems classically encounters exponential bottlenecks, which quantum devices circumvent by natively encoding wavefunctions. In the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, however, hardware noise constrains simulation accuracy. As a stepping stone toward strongly correlated materials, we compute the band structure of 2D monolayer graphene and 1D nanoribbons (zigzag and armchair) using a single variational workflow in the $p_z$ tight-binding approximation. Non-interacting ground states also provide essential initial reference states for subspace and warm-started variational methods to solve interacting spectra. By mapping the Bloch Hamiltonian to Pauli operators, we extract the ground band via the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and excited subbands via Variational Quantum Deflation (VQD), validating our approach from ideal simulations to execution on physical IBM Quantum processors. In ideal simulations, the workflow reproduces exact diagonalization results with high precision, whereas hardware noise introduces energy deviations of a few hundredths of the hopping parameter. While qubit counts scale logarithmically with ribbon width, fixed-depth ansatz accuracy degrades with Hilbert space dimension. Crucially, deepening the ansatz improves ideal simulation accuracy by over three orders of magnitude but worsens energy estimates under noise, proving that practical circuit depth is bounded by hardware noise rather than expressivity. Finally, we complement energy evaluations with a wavefunction-level diagnostic measuring subspace containment. This diagnostic captures degenerate manifolds and exposes optimization failure modes disguised by energy agreement alone. Operating directly on NISQ hardware, this validated workflow establishes a controlled baseline for studying topological and strongly correlated phases in realistic materials.

item.title: Quint Computing Secures €9.1M ($10.2M USD) Seed Round to Scale Hardware-Level Quantum Error Correction
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article is noteworthy because Quint Computing’s approach promises to slash the number of physical qubits needed for error correction—a long‑standing bottleneck that has kept scalable superconducting processors out of reach. By using continuous electrical control to actively stabilize circuit elements, the startup could cut cryogenic heat loads and hardware overhead by up to two orders of magnitude, a leap comparable to recent advances in surface‑code optimization from IBM and Google. If the seed round and EIC Pathfinder grant translate into working prototypes, developers could see larger logical qubit counts sooner, accelerating applications such as quantum chemistry and optimization. The claim still hinges on demonstrating reliable control at scale, so experimental validation will be the next critical hurdle.

Quint Computing, a quantum hardware startup, secured €9.1 million ($10.2 million USD) in seed funding and a €2.2 million EIC Pathfinder grant. This funding will support the commercialization of their architecture, which aims to reduce physical error-correction overhead by up to 100 times. Their patented design uses continuous electrical control in superconducting circuits to stabilize individual circuit elements against noise, enabling more efficient error correction and lowering cryogenic heat loads. item.title: Substantially Improved Rate and Distance for Addressable Transversal Phase Gates
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pushes the frontier of fault‑tolerant quantum computing by delivering explicit families of error‑correcting codes that combine a higher encoding rate and larger relative distance with fully addressable transversal non‑Clifford phase gates—a rare combination that has long been limited to modest parameters. By moving beyond binary CSS constructions and using cyclic, algebraic‑geometric techniques, the authors raise the asymptotic lower bound on both rate and distance to roughly 0.077 / h and even tighten it further with an exponential‑time construction, narrowing the gap to a newly derived universal upper limit. The concrete 48‑ and 90‑qubit codes for transversal T gates give hardware designers realistic benchmarks for building more efficient logical layers while highlighting that further gains will still require clever code design or trade‑offs in compilation overhead.

An important ingredient in fault-tolerant quantum computation is asymptotically good codes with fully addressable transversal non-Clifford gates. Existing constructions, however, provide only small explicit guarantees for rate and relative distance. Here, we substantially improve these guarantees for fully addressable transversal phase gates at every fixed level $h\ge3$ of the Clifford hierarchy, using a cyclic encoding beyond the binary CSS framework. The encoding separates logical phase control from the joint design of rate and distance, enabling two constructions with different computational costs. A deterministic polynomial-time algebraic-geometric construction gives a common asymptotic lower bound of $52/(675h)$ on both quantities. A counting argument gives an exponential-time construction with exact verification, improving this bound by a factor of approximately $2.86$. We further establish a universal upper bound for codes supporting fully addressable transversal single-qubit phase gates. Within our cyclic encoding framework, we obtain a stronger upper bound that is approximately $1.28$ times the lower bound achieved by our exponential-time construction. As concrete examples, we construct codes with $48$ and $90$ physical qubits supporting fully addressable transversal $T$ gates. These results narrow the gap between achievable code parameters and addressability bounds, providing quantitative targets for further improvements in efficient code constructions.

item.title: Conditional Quantum Priors for Chaotic Fluid Dynamics
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a single quantum‑generated prior can be conditioned on system parameters such as the Reynolds number, letting classical neural networks inherit accurate long‑term statistical information without retraining for each new flow regime. By cutting the required trainable weights by roughly 85 % and halving the Jensen–Shannon divergence on Lorenz‑63, the work demonstrates a concrete efficiency boost that aligns with the broader push toward hybrid quantum‑classical machine‑learning pipelines for physics problems. The photonic NISQ implementation further proves the approach is viable on near‑term hardware, suggesting a practical route to more reliable turbulence forecasting once larger quantum devices become available.

Neural networks that predict chaotic dynamics can reproduce short trajectories while misrepresenting statistics over long times. Quantum priors represent selected dynamical statistics through quantum generative models and provide statistical constraints for classical neural networks. Training a separate prior for each value of a system parameter, such as the Reynolds number, does not explicitly model how these statistics vary with that parameter. We learn a conditional quantum prior that approximates selected statistics of an invariant measure at unseen parameter values within the training range, without retraining. For Lorenz-63, the prior reduces mean Jensen-Shannon divergence by 56.9% relative to a classical multilayer perceptron with a comparable number of weights across 96 unseen parameter values. Across 101 values of the same parameter, the shared prior uses 84.7% fewer trainable weights than would be required by a separate quantum neural network at each value. We then use the learned prior to regularize classical neural networks, encouraging their autoregressive rollouts to better reproduce long-term statistics. For Kolmogorov flow at Reynolds number $Re=1000$, prior regularization reduces forecast mean squared error by 66.0% over 318 steps relative to the classical baseline without prior regularization. We also implement a photonic quantum prior for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, achieving a mean Jensen-Shannon divergence of $4.58\times10^{-3}$ for Lorenz-63 and $2.59\times10^{-3}$ for Kolmogorov flow at unseen parameter values.

item.title: Autonomous cooling of Kerr-cat qubits to minutes-long bit-flip times
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that Kerr‑cat qubits can be autonomously cooled via a resonant lossy mode, extending their intrinsic bit‑flip lifetime from milliseconds to minutes (up to 450 s) while preserving fast Z gates and high‑fidelity single‑shot readout. By confirming the predicted exponential scaling of flip times with photon number, the work pushes biased‑noise hardware‑efficient error correction into a regime where logical qubits could be built with dramatically lower overhead than conventional superconducting transmons. The result shows that the remaining bottleneck is now phase‑flip loss rather than bit‑flips, highlighting a clear path toward more practical fault‑tolerant quantum processors.

Quantum error correction becomes more hardware efficient when physical noise is strongly biased towards one error channel. Cat qubits realize such a bias by encoding information in two opposite coherent states of a superconducting oscillator, so that bit flips are exponentially suppressed with photon number while phase-flip rates increase only linearly. In Kerr-cat qubits, a driven double-well potential confines these states and enables fast coherent control, but excitations can induce interwell switching, limiting bit-flip times to milliseconds. Here we show that the nonlinear interaction generating the confinement can also cool these excitations. When an intra-well transition becomes resonant with a lossy readout mode, excitations are transferred out of the qubit and dissipated, as established by spectroscopy and relaxation measurements. We observe the predicted exponential scaling of Kerr-cat bit-flip times with photon number, reaching 450 s, over five orders of magnitude beyond previous demonstrations. Phase-flip rates remain consistent with intrinsic photon loss at operating points with seconds-long bit-flip times. We further demonstrate fast Z gates without measurable degradation of bit-flip protection and single-shot readout with a bit-flip probability below $10^{-6}$ per measurement. Autonomous cooling thus brings minutes-long bit-flip protection to Kerr-cat qubits while retaining fast coherent control, without additional cooling drives or circuit elements.

item.title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing Detection with Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that a hybrid quantum‑classical recurrent network can match—and on a tiny dataset even surpass—state‑of‑the‑art classical RNNs while using orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters and only a handful of qubits, highlighting the efficiency gains possible with variational quantum models. It builds on recent advances in quantum machine learning that have shown promise for static classification tasks, extending them to real‑world time‑series data such as sleep‑disordered breathing detection. The results suggest that, once more robust hardware and error mitigation techniques become available, quantum recurrent architectures could offer compact, low‑power alternatives for edge‑deployed health monitoring and other sequential inference problems.

This work investigates the application of Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks to the binary classification of sleep-disordered breathing events in time-series data, aiming to distinguish between apneic and normal breathing episodes. A variational classical--quantum architecture is proposed and evaluated against classical Recurrent Neural Network models. Experiments were conducted on multiple real-world datasets with varying levels of complexity to assess the strengths and limitations of the quantum approach. In the comparative analysis, both classical and quantum models showed comparable performance. The quantum model achieved superior performance on the smallest dataset, while yielding slightly weaker results in the most complex setting. However, the quantum approach exhibited notable strengths, such as competitive performance despite a drastically reduced parameter count and low-qubit regime, as well as good generalization capabilities. These results suggest that, despite current hardware and algorithmic limitations, variational quantum recurrent models represent a promising alternative for time-series classification as Quantum Computing technologies continue to mature.
